references.text: Earlier in the same chapter, the command is given to appoint cities of refuge where someone who kills another by accident can flee and be protected from the avenger of blood until the case is tried before the assembly.
Joshua describes the same cities of refuge that were appointed for the Israelites, the foreigner, and the resident alien, so that anyone who kills another by accident may flee there.
The basis for the cities of refuge is found here, where it speaks of a place God will designate for someone who did not intend to kill but did so accidentally.
Moses gives detailed instructions about the cities of refuge, including that they must be accessible to anyone who kills their neighbor without intent, and that the innocent must not die.
Moses set apart three cities on the east side of the Jordan as cities of refuge for someone who had killed their neighbor unintentionally and without prior hostility.
The command to treat the foreigner as a native and love them as oneself is reflected in the fact that the cities of refuge were also available to foreigners and resident aliens.
The law concerning sin committed accidentally (בִּשְׁגָגָה) applies both to the native Israelite and to the foreigner living among them, the same principle found in the law of the cities of refuge.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of fleeing to seize the hope set before us, an image that can be linked to those who fled to the cities of refuge to find protection.
